Last updated: 12 May 2026. Version 1.0.

This Privacy Policy explains how Booming Venture handles personal data. We follow the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Dutch implementation (Uitvoeringswet AVG), and the ePrivacy obligations in the Dutch Telecommunicatiewet. If anything below is unclear, email info@boomingventure.com and we will rewrite it.

1. Who we are

Booming Venture is the data controller for personal data collected through this website.

  • Address: Breedveldsingel 1, 3055 PG Rotterdam, The Netherlands
  • Email: info@boomingventure.com
  • KvK (Chamber of Commerce): [to be added]
  • VAT (BTW): [to be added]

We have not appointed a Data Protection Officer. Our processing does not meet the thresholds in GDPR Article 37(1), but you can reach our privacy contact at the email above.

2. What personal data we collect

  • Identification and contact data you give us: name, work email, company, role, phone (optional).
  • Communication content: the message you send via the contact form, support emails, chatbot transcripts.
  • Billing data for clients: invoicing details and VAT identifiers.
  • Website usage data: IP address, browser, device, pages viewed, referrer, time on page. Most of this is collected by Google Analytics in pseudonymous form.
  • Marketing data for clients: campaign performance numbers on platforms we manage for you. This is processed under a separate Data Processing Agreement.
  • Lead-magnet data: the email you enter to download the Growth Guide or UNIFY Framework guide, plus the source field.

3. Why we process it and the legal basis

  • To deliver the services you hire us for. Legal basis: performance of a contract (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR).
  • To respond to your enquiry and follow up. Legal basis: legitimate interest in answering people who contact us (Art. 6(1)(f)). You can object at any time.
  • To send marketing emails to subscribers and existing clients. Legal basis: consent for new subscribers (Art. 6(1)(a) plus Telecommunicatiewet art. 11.7), or the soft opt-in for existing clients who can unsubscribe from every email.
  • To improve the website and security. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f)), with a balancing test on record.
  • To comply with tax law. Legal basis: legal obligation, seven-year retention under Algemene wet inzake rijksbelastingen art. 52.

4. Cookies and similar trackers

Cookies that are strictly necessary for the site to work (session, security, load balancing) run by default. Every other cookie, including analytics, marketing pixels, and the DataSpeak chat, only loads after you accept it through the consent banner. You can change or withdraw consent any time via the cookie button in the footer.

The categories we use:

  • Strictly necessary: WordPress session, cookie-consent record, Cloudflare bot mitigation.
  • Analytics: Google Analytics 4 via Google Tag Manager. Pseudonymous user ID, page views, events. 14-month retention.
  • Marketing: Brevo tracking pixel for email engagement on opt-in lists.
  • Functional: DataSpeak conversational AI cookies when the chatbot is opened.

5. Who we share data with

We use the following processors. Each has a Data Processing Agreement with us under GDPR Article 28.

  • Brevo (Sendinblue SAS, France) for transactional and marketing email.
  • DataSpeak B.V. (Netherlands) for the website chatbot.
  • Google Ireland Ltd for Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager. Data flows to Google LLC in the United States.
  • Cloudflare Inc. for content delivery and security.
  • Our WordPress hosting provider.

We do not sell personal data and we do not share it for cross-context behavioural advertising.

6. Transfers outside the EU/EEA

Google and Cloudflare process data in the United States. Both companies are certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Commission adequacy decision of 10 July 2023). As a fallback we rely on Standard Contractual Clauses (Commission Decision 2021/914) and we have transfer impact assessments on file. You can request a copy by emailing us.

7. How long we keep data

  • Client engagement records and invoicing: 7 years after the contract ends (tax obligation).
  • Prospect and lead data: 24 months from the last interaction.
  • Newsletter subscribers: until unsubscribe plus 30 days of suppression-list retention.
  • Chatbot transcripts: 12 months.
  • Google Analytics: 14 months (default).
  • Server logs: 14 days for security forensics.

8. Your rights

Under GDPR you can:

  • Request a copy of the personal data we hold (right of access, Art. 15).
  • Correct inaccurate data (Art. 16).
  • Ask us to delete data when there is no longer a legal reason to keep it (Art. 17).
  • Ask us to restrict processing while a dispute is resolved (Art. 18).
  • Receive your data in a portable format (Art. 20).
  • Object to processing based on legitimate interest (Art. 21).
  • Withdraw consent at any time without losing the lawfulness of past processing (Art. 7(3)).

Email info@boomingventure.com to use any of these rights. We respond within one month (Art. 12(3)). You also have the right to file a complaint with the Dutch supervisory authority, Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens.

9. Automated decisions and AI tools

The Funnel Leak Calculator and ROI Forecaster on this site produce estimates based on the numbers you type in. They do not store your inputs, do not profile you, and do not make any decision that has a legal or similarly significant effect on you. The DataSpeak chatbot is an AI system, and you will see a disclosure that you are chatting with one before the conversation starts.

For client work, any automated profiling we run on a campaign is governed by the Data Processing Agreement with that client.

10. Security

The site uses TLS in transit. Access to admin systems is restricted and logged. Passwords are hashed. Backups are encrypted. We test our defences regularly.

11. Data breaches

If a breach poses a risk to your rights, we notify the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens within 72 hours under Art. 33 GDPR. If the risk is high, we notify you directly under Art. 34.

12. Children

Our services are aimed at businesses. We do not knowingly collect data from anyone under 16.

13. Changes to this policy

We update this page when our processing changes or when the law does. The version date at the top tells you when. For material changes that affect existing subscribers, we send an email.

item.title: What is AI marketing? (And why it’s not just hype)
item.excerpt:encoded: AI marketing isn’t just a buzzword — it’s a fundamental shift in how we understand and engage customers. Discover the data-driven strategies that are transforming business growth.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

AI marketing is the use of machine learning, language models, and predictive analytics to make every step of the customer journey faster, sharper, and more personal. It is an operating model, not a tool you buy. Done well, it changes how you target, write, score, send, and report. Done badly, it gives you faster spam.

Ask ten marketers what AI marketing means and you will get ten answers. Most of them are vague. That is fine for cocktail conversations and bad for budgets, so this article gives you a working definition, a list of what counts and what does not, and the parts of the marketing stack where AI actually moves the number.

A working definition

AI marketing is the systematic use of machine learning, generative models, and predictive analytics to do three things faster than humans alone could: understand the customer, decide what to send them, and produce the content that lands. The systematic part matters. One ChatGPT prompt does not make a marketing program AI-driven. A workflow that scores leads, drafts variations, A/B tests them, and feeds the result back into the model does.

The shift is structural. Five years ago, a CRM segmentation was a SQL query a marketer wrote on Monday and forgot by Friday. Today, the same segmentation updates itself every time someone opens an email or stalls in checkout. The marketer's job moved from authoring rules to designing the loop.

Why this happened now

Three changes between 2022 and 2025 made the difference.

  • Inference got cheap. Running a useful language model on a single email used to cost ten cents. It is closer to a tenth of that now. That makes per-customer personalisation a budget line, not a science project.
  • First-party data got better. The death of third-party cookies forced brands to invest in their own data layer. Once you have one, AI has something to chew on.
  • Attribution stopped lying. Marketing-mix modelling and incrementality testing replaced last-click in most credible teams. AI loves a stable training signal, and revenue is one.

What counts as AI marketing and what doesn't

The honest test is whether the system learns from outcomes. Most martech features called "AI" do not.

  • Counts. Predictive lead scoring trained on closed-won data. Generative subject-line testing where the winners feed the model. RFM models that update each week. Dynamic landing pages that select hero copy by visitor intent. Look-alike audiences built from your highest-LTV cohorts. Conversational chat that uses live product data.
  • Does not count. A static "AI rewrite this paragraph" button. Email send-time optimisation based on a single rule. Vendor demos where the AI feature is a dashboard label. ChatGPT pasted into Notion.

The market is full of the second list because the first is harder to sell. Vendors slap "AI" on a feature flag because procurement responds to it. You can see through this in fifteen minutes: ask how the model is trained, what data it uses, and what happens to the output when a customer responds. If the answers are fuzzy, the feature is decoration.

Where AI actually moves the number

The wins concentrate in four places. We see this across the engagements we run at Booming Venture, and the pattern repeats in industry data from HubSpot's State of Marketing and McKinsey's annual AI surveys.

1. Lead scoring

Replacing manual lead scoring with a model trained on your own closed-won and closed-lost data typically lifts SQL-to-customer conversion 15 to 30 percent. The reason is dull: humans build scoring rules around the leads they remember. Models look at all of them.

2. Content variation at scale

If you run paid search or paid social with more than 50 ad groups, AI-generated ad copy variations beat static creative within two to three weeks. The trick is not the generation, it is the workflow that promotes winners and kills losers automatically.

3. Email and lifecycle

Subject-line testing, send-time optimisation, and segment selection all benefit. Open rates and click rates rise. Revenue per email rises only when product recommendations are personalised based on actual behaviour, not catalogue order.

4. Reporting and decisioning

The least glamorous use case earns the biggest ROI. Models that watch your data daily and surface anomalies, drops, and opportunities save a senior analyst's week, every week. The investment pays back in months.

Where it does not (yet)

Long-form thought leadership content. AI drafts read like AI drafts to anyone who reads a lot. Same for brand voice work, podcasts, and any place where the human is the product. Treat AI as the research analyst and the typing pool, not the columnist.

How to start without burning a year

Three steps, in order. They are deliberately small.

  1. Pick one decision that gets made often and badly. Lead scoring is the usual answer for B2B. For B2C, it is product recommendations on the cart page.
  2. Get the data right before you get the model right. AI fails for the same reason BI fails: dirty inputs. Spend the first month on the data layer.
  3. Set up the loop. Outputs, outcomes, feedback. If you cannot trace from a model decision to a revenue change, you have a demo, not a program.

Use the Funnel Leak Calculator to see which stage in your funnel is leaking the most revenue, then point the first AI project at that stage. Fixing the worst leak first compounds the budget you have for the next experiment.

Frequently asked questions

Is AI marketing different from marketing automation?

Yes. Automation runs predefined rules. AI marketing chooses what to do based on signals the rules did not anticipate.

Do I need a data scientist?

Not for the starter wins. Modern tools (HubSpot AI, Klaviyo predictive analytics, Customer.io's AI features) ship usable models out of the box. You need a data scientist when you start training models on your own data, which is usually year two.

What does AI marketing cost?

The licence cost is the small line. The work to clean data, design the loop, and edit AI output is the real budget. Plan for a 70/30 split between people and software.

What about the EU AI Act?

Most marketing AI is "limited risk" under Article 50 of Regulation 2024/1689. You disclose that users are interacting with an AI system (chatbots) and mark AI-generated content. Article 50 transparency obligations apply from August 2026.

The bottom line

AI marketing is not a category of tools. It is an operating model where decisions get faster and more personal because a learning system sits inside the workflow. Start with the worst leak in your funnel. Pick one model. Build the loop. Then expand.

item.title: 7 biggest growth mistakes premium brands make
item.excerpt:encoded: Premium brands often fall into growth traps that commoditize their positioning. Learn the 7 critical mistakes and how to avoid them while scaling sustainably.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Premium brands lose more growth to commodity thinking than to competitors. The seven mistakes below are the patterns we see most often: discounting reflexes, chasing volume, broken positioning, wrong channels, lazy creative, weak retention, and no measurement. Fix the worst two first.

Premium has a margin problem only when growth gets sloppy. The brands that scale without losing pricing power keep doing the boring work: protecting position, choosing fewer customers better, and refusing the shortcuts that look like growth on a dashboard.

We have audited dozens of premium brands across fashion, B2B SaaS, professional services, and consumer products. The same seven mistakes show up. Here they are, ranked by how often they bite.

1. The discounting reflex

The first instinct when revenue dips is a promotion. Premium brands feel this instinct too, and most give in once. The cost is not the discount, it is the new anchor price. Customers who bought at 30% off treat the discounted price as the real one and wait for the next sale.

If you must discount, do it under a different brand name, on a private list, with a time-bound mechanism that does not become a pattern. Better: bundle, upgrade, or add a limited service tier instead.

2. Chasing volume in the wrong room

Premium positioning assumes scarcity. The moment you optimise for monthly orders, the rest of the strategy bends. Paid traffic gets cheaper but it brings the wrong audience. Influencers get bigger but they sit further from your buyer. Email lists grow but open rates fall.

Track quality of growth alongside volume. A useful metric is the ratio of new customer LTV to acquired CAC at the cohort level. If new cohorts are cheaper to acquire but worth less, you have growth on paper and decline in reality.

3. Positioning drift

Founders ship a brand. The team grows. New marketers join. They each rewrite the homepage a little. Three years in, the brand sounds like every other brand in the category.

The fix is a brand book that is short, opinionated, and used. Twelve pages beats sixty. Include the one sentence that explains why anyone should pay 2x. Test every piece of new copy against it.

4. The wrong channel mix

Premium brands inherit best practice from mass-market playbooks. They run Meta lookalikes, broad keyword campaigns, and influencer mass-marketing. None of these tools are wrong, the targeting is.

Audit the channel mix against the actual buyer journey. Premium B2B buyers research on LinkedIn, podcasts, and trade publications. Premium consumers come from PR, peer recommendations, and high-intent search. Spend follows attention, not the other way around.

5. Lazy creative

Premium creative is the highest-leverage line on the P&L and the one most often outsourced to whoever bids lowest. The work has to look like the price.

If you are running performance creative, ship 3 to 5 new variations weekly, treat the brand as the constant and the message as the variable, and reject anything that could have been written for a competitor.

6. No retention machine

Acquisition gets the attention. Retention pays the bills. Premium customers churn quietly: one cancelled invoice, one delayed reorder, one quiet unsubscribe. By the time the dashboard shows it, six months are gone.

Build a retention loop with a named owner. Weekly review of churn signals, a 30-60-90 day post-purchase sequence, and a quarterly check-in for top tier customers. Use the Funnel Leak Calculator to size the cost of your current churn rate.

7. Vibes-based measurement

Premium brands often measure brand by gut and performance by last click. Neither tells the truth. Without a basic marketing-mix model or an incrementality framework, every channel argues for more budget and no channel can prove it.

Start with the simplest test: a geographic holdout for paid media. Run it for 30 days. The result is usually that the agency-favourite channel is over-credited and an underfunded channel is dramatically more efficient.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to fix these?

Positioning and creative can shift in a quarter. Retention and measurement take six to twelve months because they touch culture, not just process.

Which one matters most?

For most premium brands we work with, retention is the largest unfixed problem. It compounds faster than any acquisition channel.

Should premium brands run paid ads at all?

Yes, but with tight intent matching. Branded search and high-intent retargeting beat broad prospecting nine times out of ten.

Pick two mistakes from this list. Fix them in 90 days. Ignore the other five until you have. Most growth-stage premium brands try to fix everything at once and end up moving none of them.

item.title: Why traditional marketing strategies fail in 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: The marketing playbook from 2020 is obsolete. Consumer behavior, technology, and market dynamics have fundamentally shifted. Here’s what works now.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

The 2020 marketing playbook breaks in 2025 because three things changed at once: third-party tracking died, AI Overviews ate the top of search, and buyers got faster than your funnel. The fix is to design for first-party data, short attention, and signal-based selling rather than rule-based campaigns.

Marketing teams that ran the same playbook in 2025 that worked in 2020 quietly underperformed for two years. The pipeline still showed leads. The dashboard still showed conversions. The number that mattered, revenue per dollar of marketing spend, fell. Here is why, and what to do instead.

The three changes that broke the old playbook

Third-party data shrunk to nothing useful

Apple's ATT prompt, Safari's tracking-prevention defaults, and Chrome's gradual cookie removal eliminated the targeting precision that made 2018 to 2021 performance marketing work. Look-alike audiences degraded. Retargeting reach collapsed on iOS. CPMs rose because every advertiser was guessing at the same person.

Search changed shape

Google's AI Overviews and similar features at Bing and Perplexity compress top-of-funnel queries into a single answer box. Informational click-through rates dropped 30 to 60 percent on the queries where Overviews show, depending on category. If your blog strategy was "answer common questions and get free traffic", the traffic is no longer free.

Buyers cut their own funnel

Modern B2B buyers complete 60 to 80 percent of the buying process before they speak to sales. They watch competitors on G2, read reviews on Reddit, listen to a podcast, and arrive at the demo with a shortlist. The marketing job is not to fill the top of a long funnel any more, it is to be on the shortlist before the buyer admits they have a project.

What still works

Three things still produce predictable results.

  • Brand at the top. Branded search volume is the most reliable forward indicator of pipeline. Invest in being the brand people search for, not just the one Google decides to serve.
  • First-party data systems. A customer data platform tied to email and CRM gives you the targeting precision that third-party cookies used to provide. The investment is real (six figures for mid-market), the alternative is invisible.
  • Trust signals at high-intent moments. Case studies, named customer logos, peer reviews, and security pages convert in 2025 because trust is what is rare. The buyer can find features anywhere.

What stopped working

  • Last-click attribution. Use marketing-mix modelling or incrementality testing instead. Last-click systematically over-credits paid search and underfunds brand and PR.
  • Long nurture emails to cold lists. Engagement died after 2022. Cold acquisition email is still effective but only with sender warming, segmentation, and short copy.
  • Generic gated content. If the ebook says what every ebook says, gating costs you the signal it provides. Either make it specific or make it free.

What to build instead

  1. A demand layer above the funnel. Podcast, LinkedIn presence from named people, ungated content. Measured by branded search lift and direct traffic, not lead form fills.
  2. A signal layer. Track when accounts view pricing, return to the site, or hit the comparison page. Pass those signals to sales the same day.
  3. An automation layer. Lifecycle email tied to behaviour, not time. AI-driven scoring and routing. Quarterly model retraining.

This stack is harder to set up than the 2020 funnel, and once it works it is more durable. We help mid-market clients implement it in 90-day phases through the UNIFY Framework.

Frequently asked questions

How long until I see results from the new playbook?

Brand and demand investments take two to four quarters to show in pipeline. Signal-based selling moves the number in 30 to 60 days because you are reallocating effort, not building new audiences.

Do I need to fire my paid agency?

Probably not. Most agencies can run signal-based playbooks if you give them the signals. The question is whether they still measure last-click on the dashboard. If yes, change the dashboard.

Is SEO dead?

No. The middle and bottom of the funnel are growing on search even as informational top-of-funnel shrinks. Optimise for comparison, alternative, and pricing queries.

The new playbook is less linear than the old one. It works because buyers stopped being linear. Run the ROI Forecaster against your current and proposed channel mix to see the shift in cost-of-acquisition before you commit to the change.

item.title: How AI automation strengthens (not replaces) your marketing team
item.excerpt:encoded: AI isn’t here to replace marketers — it’s here to amplify their capabilities. Discover how smart automation can free your team to focus on strategy and creativity.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

AI does not replace marketers, it absorbs the work marketers should never have been doing. Used well, it raises the floor on output quality and frees the team to do the strategic work that actually compounds. Used badly, it makes mediocre faster.

Every marketing leader gets the same question from their CMO right now: how is AI changing your team's headcount plan? The honest answer is that AI is changing what the team does, not how many people you need. The composition of the work is the part to watch.

The work AI absorbs

Three categories of marketing work shift to AI in 2025 without controversy.

  • Variant production. Twenty ad headlines, ten email subject lines, twelve image prompts. AI is faster than any human at producing the long tail of variants that performance marketing eats.
  • Translation and localisation. First-pass translation across five EU languages, then human edit. Cost falls 60 to 80 percent. Quality holds if the editor is a native speaker.
  • Data summarisation. Weekly dashboard read-outs, anomaly callouts, account-level briefings before sales calls. Marketers spend less time pasting numbers into Slack.

The work AI does not absorb (yet)

The strategic layer stays human.

  • Brand voice and positioning.
  • Original research and proprietary data analysis.
  • Customer relationships and account-level strategy.
  • Editorial judgement on what to publish and what to kill.
  • Negotiation with platforms, partners, and internal stakeholders.

If your job is one of these, AI makes you better. If your job is mostly variant production, the job description changes.

How team composition shifts

Three years from now, healthy mid-market marketing teams will look like this.

  • Fewer pure execution roles. The junior who used to write 20 versions of the same ad is now a strategist editing AI outputs.
  • More analysts. Someone has to design the feedback loops, measure what works, and retrain the models.
  • Same number of writers. The good ones publish more. The mediocre ones get replaced by AI plus a senior editor.
  • One AI lead. Either a hire or a third of a senior marketer's time. Owns the AI roadmap, the tool stack, and the prompt library.

How to introduce AI without breaking culture

  1. Start with a single workflow. Lead scoring, subject-line testing, or content briefs. Get one win before broadening.
  2. Run AI side by side with the team for one quarter. Compare output. Show the team the data. Trust grows from seeing the work, not from a town hall slide.
  3. Pay for senior, save on junior. The mistake we see most often is shipping AI output without senior editing. The work gets worse and the brand suffers.
  4. Publish your AI use policy. Be explicit with your team and your customers about what gets AI assistance and what does not. The EU AI Act will require some of this in 2026 anyway.

What this looks like in practice

A B2B SaaS team of seven we work with shifted in 2024 from 70 percent execution and 30 percent strategy to roughly 40 percent execution and 60 percent strategy. Headcount stayed the same. Published content volume tripled. Pipeline grew 38 percent. The two changes that mattered most were a custom GPT for content briefs and a Klaviyo-based lifecycle setup tied to product usage signals.

Frequently asked questions

Will junior marketers still get hired?

Yes, but the role looks different. Less hand production, more output editing, more analytical work. The strongest juniors learn to direct AI rather than compete with it.

How do I know if my AI use is making content worse?

Measure engagement at the cohort level. If your AI-assisted content has lower scroll depth and email reply rate than your human-only baseline, the editing is too thin.

What is the right budget split for AI tools?

For mid-market, 8 to 15 percent of the marketing tools budget is the current band. Heavily skewed toward Copilot or Gemini for the team and one or two specialised tools for content or analysis.

The teams that thrive in this transition treat AI as a senior intern, not a replacement. Give it the right work, edit its output, measure the difference, and free your humans to do the things that compound.

item.title: The future of content: AI as your creative assistant
item.excerpt:encoded: Content creation is evolving beyond human vs. AI to human + AI collaboration.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

The argument about AI versus human content is over. The winning teams treat AI as a creative assistant that compresses the boring parts of writing. The output that ranks and converts is human voice plus AI speed.

Two years ago marketers asked whether AI could write their content. Today the question is what jobs AI does best inside a content workflow that still has humans at the top and bottom. Here is the breakdown we use with clients, with what works and what does not.

What AI does brilliantly

  • Research compression. Twenty competitor articles summarised in five minutes, with claims tagged for verification.
  • Outline generation. Take a topic, target keyword, and intent, get a usable structure in seconds. Edit the structure, not the blank page.
  • Variant production. Ten ad headlines, six email subject lines, twelve CTA buttons. AI is faster than any human and the lift over a single creative is real.
  • Translation drafts. First-pass localisation across five EU languages, then native edit.
  • Metadata. Meta descriptions, image alt text, schema markup. The work no one wants to do.

What AI still cannot do well

  • Original opinions. AI writes what is common, by definition.
  • Specific personal stories. The detail that makes content stick comes from real life.
  • Voice consistency over long pieces. Subtle voice drift creeps in after 800 words.
  • Original research. AI cannot run a survey, interview a customer, or do regression analysis with judgement.

The workflow that works

  1. Human brief. Topic, angle, target reader, three claims to support. 15 minutes.
  2. AI research and outline. Use ChatGPT, Claude, or a tool like Surfer to surface sources and structure. 10 minutes.
  3. Human voice pass. Write the introduction, the conclusion, and any section that needs an opinion or story. 60 minutes.
  4. AI fill-in. Draft the procedural sections (the 'here are five steps' parts). 5 minutes.
  5. Human edit pass. Trim, sharpen, add specific examples, fix voice. 30 minutes.
  6. AI utility pass. Meta description, alt text, FAQ schema. 5 minutes.

Total: about two hours for a 1500-word piece. A skilled human-only writer takes four to six. A pure AI piece takes 20 minutes and reads like a pure AI piece.

How to keep the AI voice out of the published version

The patterns to watch for and edit ruthlessly:

  • Triads ("X, Y, and Z") stacked in consecutive sentences.
  • Sentences of similar length in a row. Vary aggressively.
  • Banned phrases: "in today's fast-paced world", "navigate the complexities", "unlock the potential", "harness the power of".
  • Symmetry. AI loves balanced structures. Break them.
  • Vague hyperbole. Replace with a number.

The honest trade-off

Content quality at the top end is now slightly easier and dramatically more crowded. Distribution matters more, opinion matters more, and original research matters more. The cheap end of content is now nearly free, which means it is also nearly worthless for search rankings.

If your content strategy was based on volume, it is breaking. If it was based on point of view, AI gives you compounding leverage.

Frequently asked questions

Does Google penalise AI-assisted content?

No. Google's policy is about helpful content, not authorship. AI-assisted content that is reviewed, accurate, and useful ranks fine. Pure scaled AI spam gets demoted.

Should I disclose AI assistance?

Most publications now have AI use policies. We disclose when AI does substantial drafting work, do not disclose when it only assists with research or metadata.

How many pieces a week can a small team publish?

With this workflow, one mid-sized team can ship 5 to 8 well-edited 1500-word pieces a week. That is more than most teams can promote, so distribution is usually the new bottleneck.

The future of content is humans and AI in the right order. The writer is still the writer. The assistant just got faster.

item.title: Integrating branding with performance marketing for sustainable growth
item.excerpt:encoded: The false choice between brand building and performance marketing is killing long-term growth.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Brand and performance marketing are treated as separate teams with separate budgets in most companies. That split costs growth. The integrated model is to measure brand investments by their effect on performance metrics over time, and to keep performance creative on-brand.

The 60/40 brand-to-performance split that the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute popularised is a starting point, not a rule. The real question is whether your brand and performance work are reinforcing each other or running in parallel.

Most companies run them in parallel. Brand is the team that books out-of-home and does the rebrand every three years. Performance is the team that runs Meta ads and gets shouted at when CAC rises. They share a CMO and not much else.

Why the split costs growth

Three failures are common.

  • Performance creative drifts off-brand. The fastest-converting ad copy is often the most generic. Without brand guard-rails, performance teams optimise for tactical wins that erode positioning.
  • Brand work gets measured wrong, or not at all. Tracking lift in branded search, direct traffic, and aided recall is uncommon. The brand team defaults to creative awards, not commerce.
  • Budgets shift to whatever can be measured this quarter. Performance always wins this argument because the dashboard is real and the brand-lift study is annual.

Three signals that brand and performance are integrated

  1. Branded search volume is on the weekly dashboard. If brand spend increases, branded search rises 4 to 12 weeks later. If branded search is flat or falling, your brand investment is not landing.
  2. Performance teams use the same brand book as brand teams. Tone, colour, type, messaging. Performance can produce more variants, but the brand bar holds.
  3. Marketing-mix modelling is the planning tool, not last-click. MMM credits brand for what brand earns: the long tail of conversions that look like direct traffic.

The simple integration playbook

Five moves to align brand and performance without a reorg.

  1. Shared OKR: revenue from net-new customers, with brand and performance both accountable.
  2. Performance creative reviewed by the brand lead weekly. Not approved, just reviewed for drift.
  3. Brand campaigns measured against branded search and direct traffic, not awards.
  4. Reallocate 10 percent of performance budget per quarter to high-trust channels (PR, podcasts, sponsorships). Track effect on the same dashboard.
  5. Run a geographic incrementality test on the largest paid channel every six months. Adjust split based on results.

What this looks like in numbers

A retailer we worked with shifted from 85/15 performance/brand to 55/45 over four quarters. Branded search rose 31 percent. Blended CAC dropped 18 percent. Top-of-funnel paid efficiency improved as the audience came in warmer. Total revenue grew 22 percent in 12 months. The performance team initially resisted the shift because the dashboard they reported on showed only the performance side.

Frequently asked questions

Should small companies do brand work at all?

Yes, but cheaply. Founder-led content, partnerships, and earned media count. The mistake is to treat brand as something only big companies can afford.

How long until brand investments show in performance?

Four to twelve weeks for branded search lift. Six to twelve months for sustained CAC improvement.

Who owns the integration?

The CMO, or the most senior marketer on the team. Without one accountable owner, the split persists.

The brands that grow most reliably in 2025 do not pick brand or performance. They run both with the same dashboard. See how we structure this for mid-market clients.

item.title: AI marketing for B2B: opportunities, risks, and real results
item.excerpt:encoded: B2B marketing is ripe for AI transformation, but the stakes are higher.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

AI marketing in B2B is messier than in B2C because the sales cycle is longer, the decision-makers are committees, and one bad output reaches procurement. The biggest wins are in account research, lead scoring, and outbound personalisation. The biggest risks are hallucinations in customer-facing material and weak data hygiene.

B2B marketers got a slower start with AI than their B2C peers, for a fair reason: more is at stake per touchpoint. A bad ad headline costs a click. A hallucinated stat in an enterprise sales deck costs the deal. Here is where the leverage is real and where the caution is justified.

Where AI moves the number in B2B

1. Account research

Tools that summarise a target company's 10-K, recent press, exec moves, and tech stack save hours per account. SDRs go into calls warmer, AEs send more relevant follow-ups, marketing produces account-specific landing pages at scale.

2. Lead scoring

Trained on your own closed-won and closed-lost data, predictive scoring beats hand-built rules by 15 to 30 percent on SQL-to-closed conversion. The win is biggest when you have at least 1,000 closed deals and clean Salesforce data.

3. Outbound personalisation

AI-drafted first lines, tied to a verified intent signal, raise reply rates from 1 to 2 percent to 4 to 8 percent in sequences we have run with B2B clients. The key is the signal, not the AI. Hand-written first lines without intent still underperform AI plus intent.

4. Content briefs and SEO

AI condenses competitive content, identifies content gaps, and structures briefs. The brief stays human-edited, the writing stays mostly human, the AI takes the busy work out.

Where the risks are real

  • Hallucinated facts in customer-facing material. Stats that do not exist, attributed quotes that were never said, regulations that were misremembered. Mitigate with verification workflow and source-grounding.
  • Brand voice drift. AI defaults to a generic professional tone. The B2B brands with distinctive voice (Drift, Gong, Intercom) lose it fast if AI output is shipped raw.
  • Data quality. AI models built on dirty CRM data make confident wrong predictions. Spend half the budget on data hygiene before the model.
  • Procurement and compliance. Enterprise buyers ask about your AI use. Have a one-pager ready. The EU AI Act's transparency rules apply from August 2026.

What good looks like

A B2B SaaS company we work with implemented three AI use cases in one quarter: predictive lead scoring (Klaviyo's model on top of HubSpot data), outbound personalisation (Clay plus a custom GPT for first lines), and AI-drafted SDR follow-ups. The combined result over 90 days: pipeline up 41 percent, average deal size up 8 percent, SDR meetings booked per day up from 1.4 to 2.8.

None of the three use cases involved AI-written long-form content. None involved a chatbot. The wins were operational, not flashy.

Where not to start

Avoid AI in customer support unless you have a high-trust deflection use case. Avoid AI-generated case studies. Avoid AI sales call summaries that go directly to the prospect. The bar for B2B trust is higher than B2C, and recovery from a bad AI interaction takes months.

Frequently asked questions

Do we need a data scientist?

Not for the starter wins. Modern tools have usable models out of the box. You need one when you train on your own data, typically year two.

How long before we see results?

Lead scoring shows up in 4 to 6 weeks. Outbound personalisation in 30 days. Account research saves time immediately but the revenue impact is harder to attribute.

What does this cost?

For a mid-market B2B team, $3K to $8K per month in tools plus the cost of one senior marketer's time to manage. Most teams already have the tools and lack the operating model.

B2B AI marketing pays back faster than most teams expect, and only when the use cases are picked carefully. Start with one workflow, prove the loop, then expand. See where your funnel is leaking before deciding which workflow to attack.

item.title: Low-hanging growth: what you can improve tomorrow using AI
item.excerpt:encoded: You don’t need a complete overhaul to see AI results.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

If you want AI results inside a month, do not start with a model. Start with three workflow changes: AI-drafted lifecycle emails, predictive subject-line testing, and dynamic product recommendations. Each lifts the metric within four weeks and costs almost nothing to test.

Most companies new to AI try to start with the impressive use cases: chatbots, content engines, predictive segmentation across the whole CRM. Those projects take six months, cost real money, and often deliver nothing for a year. Here are three that ship in four weeks.

1. AI-drafted lifecycle emails

Most lifecycle programs were written once two years ago and have not been touched since. The unsubscribe and complaint rates suggest as much. The fix is to have AI redraft each email in your lifecycle, tested against the original, with the better performer going live.

How to do it:

  1. Pull the last 12 weeks of performance data for each email in your lifecycle. Identify the bottom three by click-through.
  2. Brief AI with the goal of each email, the audience, the tone, and the offer. Ask for three variations.
  3. A/B test the best variation against the current version for 14 days. Lock in the winner.
  4. Repeat next month with the next worst-performing email.

Expected lift: 8 to 25 percent revenue per email within a quarter.

2. Predictive subject-line testing

If you run Klaviyo, HubSpot, Customer.io, or any modern ESP, the predictive subject-line feature is already in your account. Most teams have not turned it on. Switch it on for one campaign this week.

The feature scores subject lines based on historical performance from across the platform. It is not perfect, but it eliminates the worst third of bad subject lines automatically. Open rates rise 3 to 8 percent on average.

3. Dynamic product recommendations

If you run an ecommerce site, switch the static "you might also like" block on product pages and emails to an AI-driven recommender. Shopify Magic, Klaviyo product recommendations, and Algolia all do this out of the box.

Expected lift: 12 to 30 percent on attached revenue per session. The bigger your catalogue, the bigger the lift.

Three honest caveats

  • These wins compound only if you maintain them. Test losers, lock in winners, then keep testing. The cost of stagnation is the same as never starting.
  • The win comes from the loop, not the AI. A poorly run test still loses. Set up an experiment calendar, not a one-time hack.
  • Don't skip measurement. Half the teams that tell us their AI experiment failed never measured the baseline. Always have a control.

Frequently asked questions

Which of the three should I start with?

Whichever you have the cleanest baseline for. If your lifecycle is a mess, fix it first because the upside is biggest there.

Do I need new tools?

No, in most cases. The features are inside the tools you already pay for. Audit your stack before buying.

What if I have no ecommerce?

B2B equivalents: AI-drafted SDR sequences, predictive demo-show-up reminders, and AI-summarised CRM activity for AEs before calls.

Pick one. Run it for four weeks. Measure the lift. The point is not the experiment, it is showing your team that AI changes the number when it is pointed at the right workflow.

item.title: ROI optimization for Netherlands SME: a data-driven approach
item.excerpt:encoded: Dutch SMEs face unique market challenges.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Dutch SMEs face a specific ROI problem: small home market, EU privacy rules that bite, and a marketing landscape over-indexed on agencies. The wins are usually in the basics: fix your funnel before scaling spend, use first-party data well, and pick two channels you commit to.

We work with SMEs across Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Utrecht, and Eindhoven. The same patterns repeat. Dutch SMEs over-spend on paid media and under-invest in the unsexy parts of marketing that compound. Here is what we have learned about ROI optimisation in the Netherlands specifically.

Why Dutch SMEs leak more than they should

Three reasons stand out.

  • The home market is small. 17.5 million people. Paid channels saturate fast. Most B2C brands hit diminishing returns on Meta and Google within 18 months.
  • Agencies dominate execution. Many SMEs outsource all marketing to one agency. The agency's incentive is to keep doing what they did last quarter, even if a different mix would help.
  • EU privacy rules apply with teeth. The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens enforces more aggressively than most EU regulators. Tracking, consent, and cookie compliance must be solid before paid scaling makes sense.

The basics that pay back fastest

1. Fix the funnel before scaling spend

If your conversion rate is 1.2 percent and the industry average is 2.5 percent, the highest-ROI move is not more traffic. It is fixing checkout, form length, page speed, and trust signals. The same paid budget produces twice the revenue once the funnel converts at benchmark.

Use the Funnel Leak Calculator to size the missed revenue from each stage.

2. Use first-party data well

Most Dutch SMEs have email lists they barely use, CRM data they do not segment, and product usage data that never reaches marketing. Connect them. The investment is six figures or less, the payback is fast.

3. Pick two channels you commit to

A diluted budget across six channels produces nothing measurable on any of them. Commit budget to two channels you can master. For B2B SMEs the usual pair is LinkedIn plus high-intent Google search. For B2C the pair depends on category.

What does not work for Dutch SMEs

  • Trying to scale Meta forever. The Netherlands has fewer than 12 million Facebook users. Saturation comes quickly. Plan for the ceiling.
  • Generic content in Dutch. Translated US blog posts do not rank in Dutch SERPs. Original Dutch content, with Dutch examples, does.
  • Outsourcing strategy to the agency that also runs ads. The conflict of interest is too high. Keep strategy in-house, outsource execution.

A small case

A Rotterdam-based B2B services company we worked with had €40K monthly marketing spend split across six channels. Twelve months in, the spend was the same and revenue had doubled. We did three things: consolidated to LinkedIn plus Google, set up a HubSpot to Google Sheets to Looker Studio data flow, and redesigned the demo booking funnel. The funnel work alone added an estimated €420K in annual revenue.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to be on Meta?

Only if your buyer is. For most Dutch B2B and high-consideration B2C, the answer is no, or only for retargeting.

Is Dutch-language content worth it?

Yes for local-intent and SME audiences. English works fine for global B2B and tech.

How much should I spend on marketing?

Healthy benchmarks: 6 to 10 percent of revenue for B2B SMEs, 10 to 15 percent for B2C, more during growth phases.

ROI optimisation is rarely about a better channel. It is about fewer channels, run with more rigour, against a cleaner funnel.

item.title: Marketing funnel: how it works in 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: The traditional marketing funnel is dead.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

The linear marketing funnel was already wrong in 2018. In 2025 it is a useful illustration and a bad operating model. The reality is a network of intent signals from many sources, where the marketer's job is to be visible at the right moment, not to push someone down a tube.

Awareness, consideration, decision. Every textbook draws the same triangle. The textbook is wrong, but it is wrong in a useful way. The triangle is a clean model for budgeting conversations and a poor model for actual buyer behaviour.

Modern buyers move sideways and skip stages. They start at decision (they already decided they need a CRM), then move backwards (they need to convince a colleague), then to consideration (now comparing three options), then to a new awareness cycle (they realise there is a different category of tool). The funnel is more like a graph, not a tube.

What changed between 2018 and 2025

  1. Information is now infinite. Buyers can answer any question themselves. Awareness is no longer a marketer's gift to bestow.
  2. Trust collapsed. Buyers trust peers, reviews, and unaffiliated sources. They distrust ads, sales reps, and content from the brand itself.
  3. Buying committees grew. The average B2B SaaS purchase involves 6 to 11 stakeholders. The funnel is now a committee process, not an individual journey.
  4. Channels multiplied. The same buyer touches the brand on LinkedIn, Twitter, a podcast, Reddit, G2, and Google in a single research session.

A working model for 2025

Instead of a funnel, think of three states the buyer can be in, and design for each.

1. Not in market

The buyer has no project. They are not looking. The goal is to become the brand they think of when the project starts. Tools: long-form content, podcasts, thought leadership from named people, sponsorships, PR. Measurement: branded search lift, direct traffic, aided recall.

2. In market, researching

The buyer has a project. They are evaluating options. The goal is to be on the shortlist. Tools: comparison content, case studies, customer reviews on G2 or Capterra, ungated technical resources. Measurement: organic and direct traffic to comparison pages, demo requests.

3. In market, deciding

The buyer has a shortlist. They are choosing. The goal is to make it easy to say yes. Tools: high-trust signals (security pages, customer logos, named references), short demos, transparent pricing, fast follow-up from sales. Measurement: shortlist-to-close rate.

How to actually use this

  1. Map your current marketing activity to the three states. Most teams discover 80 percent of their budget is in state 3, where the smallest gains live.
  2. Reallocate 10 percent per quarter toward state 1 until you reach a healthy split (we recommend 30/40/30).
  3. Measure each state with the metrics that fit, not with last-click revenue across the board.

Why teams resist this

State 1 work has long payback. State 3 work shows results next week. Most marketing leaders have 12-month tenures and quarterly reviews. The system rewards short-termism. The brands that win invest in state 1 anyway and survive the quarter where it does not show in the dashboard.

Frequently asked questions

Is the funnel useful for anything?

Yes, for budgeting conversations with finance. They like triangles. Just do not run the team off it.

How do I measure state 1?

Branded search volume in Google Search Console, direct traffic in GA4, and a quarterly aided-awareness survey if budget allows.

What about the middle of the funnel?

It exists but it shrinks every year. Modern buyers compress evaluation. Spend less on nurture, more on signal capture.

Stop running the funnel. Start running three programs for three buyer states. Use the ROI Forecaster to model the reallocation before you commit.

item.title: The hidden costs of inefficient marketing funnels
item.excerpt:encoded: Funnel inefficiencies don’t just reduce conversions — they compound into massive hidden costs.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Funnel inefficiencies cost more than the dashboard shows. The visible cost is lower revenue. The hidden costs are higher CAC, exhausted teams, wasted ad spend, lost talent, and slower compounding. The total is usually 2 to 4x the visible loss.

Every funnel has leaks. Most teams know roughly where. Few teams know what those leaks actually cost. Here is the math behind the hidden costs of an inefficient funnel, and how to size them for your own business.

The visible cost

Take 10,000 monthly visitors, a 2 percent conversion rate, and a €500 average order value. Monthly revenue: €100K. If you fix the funnel to a 3 percent conversion rate, monthly revenue goes to €150K. That is the obvious €50K per month.

The hidden costs you ignore

1. CAC inflation

A leaky funnel pulls in more traffic to hit the same revenue. More traffic means higher CPM and CPC because you are bidding against yourself. Real-world impact: a 30 percent conversion rate gap typically translates to a 20 to 40 percent higher blended CAC.

2. Sales team thrash

Bad leads from a leaky funnel reach sales. SDRs spend hours on prospects who were never going to buy. AEs hold demos that go nowhere. A B2B sales team can lose 25 to 40 percent of productive capacity to funnel inefficiency.

3. Compounding loss

Every lost conversion is also a lost referral, lost word-of-mouth, lost LTV. Over 12 months, the compounding effect adds another 1.5 to 2x the direct revenue loss for businesses with normal retention.

4. Talent attrition

Marketing and sales teams that watch effort disappear into a broken funnel burn out. The Glassdoor-visible cost shows up as turnover. The hidden cost is the institutional knowledge that leaves with them.

5. Slower decision-making

Leaky funnels make every dashboard noisy. The team spends meetings arguing about what the numbers mean instead of fixing the problem. Six months pass.

A worked example

A SaaS company we audited had a 1.4 percent demo-request rate against an industry average of 2.8 percent. Visible cost: €120K per month in lost MRR (€1.44M annually). With hidden costs included: CAC inflation €40K/month, sales productivity loss €30K/month, compounding effect over 12 months estimated at €1M. Total annual cost of the funnel inefficiency: €3.2M. Cost to fix: €60K of consulting plus six weeks of in-house work.

How to find your hidden costs

  1. Calculate your conversion rate at each funnel stage. Compare against benchmarks. Identify the worst gap.
  2. Apply the visible cost formula. Use the Funnel Leak Calculator for the math.
  3. Multiply by 2 to estimate the all-in cost. That is the budget you can justify spending on the fix.

Frequently asked questions

How much should I spend to fix a funnel leak?

Up to half the all-in annual cost of the leak. Most teams underinvest because they only see the visible cost.

What about A/B test losses?

Properly run A/B tests are an investment, not a cost. The losses tell you what does not work. The wins compound.

Which stage usually has the biggest leak?

For B2B SaaS, the demo-to-close stage. For ecommerce, checkout. For high-consideration B2C, the form-to-lead stage.

The dashboard shows the visible cost. The hidden cost is usually 2 to 4x. Add it up before you decide what a fix is worth.

item.title: Customer retention AI strategies for 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: Acquiring customers is expensive; retaining them is profitable.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Acquisition is expensive, retention is profitable. AI changes retention by spotting churn signals before humans do, personalising lifecycle communications at scale, and predicting which customers to invest in. Three plays pay back fastest: churn prediction, lifecycle personalisation, and AI-driven win-back.

Most marketing leaders we talk to overspend on acquisition by a factor of two to four. The math is simple: a 5 percent retention lift is worth more than a 25 percent acquisition lift in most categories, and costs less to achieve. AI makes the retention work faster.

1. Predictive churn scoring

Train a model on your historical churn data. The model identifies the leading indicators: declining product usage, late payments, support tickets with negative sentiment, fewer logins from key users. Flag at-risk accounts 30 to 60 days before they would churn.

The lift comes from the intervention, not the prediction. Save 30 percent of flagged accounts and you have moved the number meaningfully. Modern tools (Gainsight, Catalyst, HubSpot's customer health score) ship usable models out of the box for B2B.

2. Lifecycle personalisation

Static lifecycle programs send the same email on day 7 to every customer. AI-driven lifecycle programs send different emails based on actual behaviour. The customer who set up the product gets advanced tips. The customer who has not logged in gets onboarding help. The customer who tried a feature and stopped gets a different sequence.

Klaviyo, Customer.io, and Iterable all offer behaviour-driven flows. Switch from time-based to behaviour-based on your three highest-volume sequences this quarter. Expected lift: 15 to 35 percent revenue per recipient.

3. AI-driven win-back

Most win-back campaigns are batch-blast generic discounts. AI-driven win-back identifies why each customer left (price, fit, competitor switch, neglect) and sends a targeted message. The reactivation rate triples in our experience.

Building this takes work: tag lost customers with churn reason, design segment-specific sequences, route responses to the right owner. Three months from start to first results.

Where AI retention does not work yet

  • Replacing human relationships for top-tier accounts. The C-suite calls and dinners still matter.
  • Predicting churn with less than 18 months of history. The model has nothing to learn from.
  • B2B retention strategies that ignore product fit. AI cannot fix a customer who never should have signed.

What to measure

  1. Gross revenue retention (the boring one, the one CFOs care about).
  2. Net revenue retention by cohort, not aggregated.
  3. Lift in retention rate from each AI intervention, measured against a hold-out control.
  4. Cost per retained customer compared to cost per acquired customer.

Frequently asked questions

Where should I start?

Predictive churn scoring, if you have at least 12 months of churn history. Lifecycle personalisation, if you do not.

How much does this cost?

Mid-market: $2K to $8K per month in tools plus one senior owner's quarter time. Enterprise: $30K to $150K per year for Gainsight-style platforms.

Will it work for B2C?

Yes, with different mechanics. Klaviyo and Bloomreach handle B2C retention well. The principles are the same: predict, personalise, intervene.

Retention is the largest unfixed problem in most marketing programs. AI lowers the cost of fixing it. Start with churn prediction, then lifecycle, then win-back.

item.title: 5 marketing automation mistakes that are losing you customers
item.excerpt:encoded: Marketing automation should nurture relationships, not damage them.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Marketing automation is supposed to scale relationships, not punish them. The five mistakes below break that promise: over-sending, generic personalisation, broken context awareness, rigid lifecycle sequences, and no handoff between automation and humans. Each one drives subscribers away.

Marketing automation platforms were sold to teams as a way to scale 1:1 communication. In practice they often scale 1:millions, badly. Here are the five mistakes that turn subscribers into unsubscribes faster than anything else.

Mistake 1: Over-sending

Every team thinks one more email cannot hurt. Every team is wrong. The breaking point varies by industry but the pattern is consistent: above 4 to 6 emails per week, list health deteriorates fast. Open rates drop, unsubscribe rates spike, spam complaints rise, and inboxes start filtering future sends.

Fix: cap weekly sends per subscriber. Use frequency suppression rules. If a customer received three campaigns in the last seven days, do not send a fourth.

Mistake 2: Generic personalisation

"Hi [First Name]" is not personalisation. Neither is dynamic content blocks that rotate through generic options. Real personalisation is sending different emails to different people based on what they have done.

Fix: segment by behaviour. Last purchase category, recent product views, lifecycle stage, NPS score, time since last purchase. Send each segment a different message, not the same message with a different name token.

Mistake 3: No context awareness

The customer just opened a support ticket. The automation sends them a survey asking how happy they are. The customer just churned. The automation sends them a renewal reminder. The customer is in the middle of a complaint. The automation sends a promotional offer.

Fix: pause automation triggers based on negative signals. Connect support, billing, and sales systems to the marketing automation. The cost is integration work, the saving is a lot of angry replies.

Mistake 4: Rigid lifecycle sequences

Many lifecycle programs are time-based and never updated. Day 1 welcome, day 3 product tour, day 7 case study, day 14 promo. The sequence ignores what the customer actually did. The customer who has used the product for two weeks gets the same emails as the customer who has not logged in once.

Fix: behaviour-driven branches. Send the day 7 email only if they actually completed the day 3 tutorial. Send the renewal reminder only if usage is healthy. Send the recovery sequence if usage drops.

Mistake 5: No handoff between automation and humans

Automation drops the conversation at exactly the moment a human should pick it up. The high-value customer replied to an automated email. The automation does not see the reply. The customer hits an account manager who does not know about the conversation. The customer becomes a former customer.

Fix: route replies. When a high-value customer replies to any automated email, surface it to the account manager that day. The investment is minimal, the retention impact is measurable.

Frequently asked questions

How many emails per week is too many?

It depends on category and engagement. For most B2C ecommerce: 3 to 5 weekly per active subscriber. For B2B newsletters: 1 weekly. Watch unsubscribe-per-send rate over 0.5 percent as a warning.

How do I test if my automation is broken?

Subscribe to your own automation under a fake account that mimics a real customer behaviour. Live in it for 30 days. The bad sequences will be obvious.

Should I scrap my automation and start over?

Rarely. Audit the five points above and fix the worst first. A full rebuild costs more than the incremental fixes earn.

Marketing automation is a force multiplier. It multiplies whatever you point at it. Point it at unsegmented, time-based, context-blind communication and it multiplies the damage. Point it at segmented, behaviour-driven, context-aware communication and it multiplies retention.

item.title: Social media ROI measurement: beyond vanity metrics
item.excerpt:encoded: Likes and follows don’t pay the bills.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Measuring social media ROI is hard because most teams measure the wrong thing. Vanity metrics (followers, likes, reach) tell you nothing about revenue. The metrics that matter are share of voice, engagement quality, conversion-attributed revenue, and influence on direct traffic. Here is how to set up each.

Every CMO eventually asks the question: what is social media earning us? The answer most agencies give is wrong because they measure what the platform reports, not what the business cares about. Here is a working framework for measuring social ROI in 2025.

What not to measure

Followers, likes, reach, and impressions tell you almost nothing. They were once useful as crude proxies for awareness. They stopped being useful when algorithms decided what gets shown. You can have 100K followers and reach 2 percent of them. Reporting reach without context is dashboard theatre.

What to measure

1. Share of voice

Track mentions of your brand against named competitors over time. Tools: Brand24, Mention, Sprout Social. Useful because it tells you whether you are growing relative to the category, not in absolute terms.

2. Engagement quality

Replies and shares from named target accounts matter more than likes from random accounts. Build a list of target accounts (in B2B, prospects and customers; in B2C, influencers and engaged buyers). Track engagement from those accounts specifically.

3. Conversion-attributed revenue

UTM-tagged links in posts and bios let you trace direct revenue. This will understate the contribution because social influence is not all click-through, but it is the floor. Set up GA4 with proper UTM hygiene.

4. Influence on direct traffic and branded search

The truest measure of social media ROI is indirect. Heavy social activity correlates with rising direct traffic and branded search 4 to 8 weeks later. Track this in GA4 and Search Console. When social spend increases, watch these numbers move.

How to attribute properly

Single-touch attribution undervalues social by 60 to 80 percent. Use one of three better methods.

  • Marketing-mix modelling. Best for budgets above €500K. Worth the investment.
  • Incrementality testing. Pause social in a holdout market for 30 days. Compare against control. Cheap and honest.
  • Post-view attribution with a long window. Less rigorous but easier. Credit conversions to social if there was a view within 14 days, even without a click.

Common pitfalls

  • Reporting follower growth without engagement context.
  • Measuring all platforms with the same dashboard. LinkedIn ROI looks different from TikTok ROI.
  • Attributing only direct conversions and concluding social does not work.
  • Treating influencer marketing the same as organic social. Different mechanics, different math.

Frequently asked questions

How long until I see ROI from organic social?

6 to 18 months for sustained results. Faster on Twitter/X, slower on LinkedIn. Plan accordingly.

Is paid social different?

Yes. Paid is easier to measure (clear click attribution) and easier to misallocate (the algorithm prefers cheap clicks, not high-value conversions). Track paid social against blended CAC, not channel-specific.

Which platform has the best ROI?

Depends on your buyer. For B2B, LinkedIn typically. For e-commerce DTC, Meta and TikTok. For high-consideration B2C, Pinterest punches above its weight.

Stop reporting vanity metrics. Pick the four KPIs above. Measure them monthly. Make budget decisions from the data, not from what the platform's account manager promises.

item.title: Advanced email marketing personalization (beyond ‘Hi [Name]’)
item.excerpt:encoded: True email personalization goes far beyond first names.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Real email personalisation goes far beyond first names. The four advanced tactics that move the number: dynamic content blocks driven by behaviour, predictive send-time per recipient, behavioural segmentation that updates daily, and product recommendations based on individual purchase patterns. Expect 30 to 60 percent lift in revenue per email.

"Hi {{First Name}}, we noticed you might be interested in..." was advanced personalisation in 2010. In 2025 it is barely table stakes. Real personalisation now means a different email goes out to every recipient, automatically, based on what they have done.

1. Dynamic content blocks

One email template, many versions. Hero image varies by predicted gender. Featured products vary by recent browse history. Tone varies by lifecycle stage. CTA varies by likely next purchase. Each recipient gets an email that looks made for them.

Tools: Klaviyo dynamic content blocks, Iterable contextual flows, Bloomreach for ecommerce. Setup is one to two weeks per campaign template, then reusable forever.

2. Predictive send-time per recipient

Sending the whole list at 9am on Tuesday is convenient for you, not them. Predictive send-time tools learn each recipient's engagement window and send to them then. Some open at 6am, some at 11pm, some on Sunday.

Lift on opens: typically 5 to 15 percent. Most major ESPs ship this as a feature now. Turn it on for one campaign this week.

3. Behavioural segmentation that updates daily

Most segmentation is static: someone is in the "newsletter" segment because they ticked a box two years ago. Better segmentation is dynamic: someone is in the "high-intent shopper" segment because they viewed a pricing page yesterday.

Set up segments that recalculate daily based on the last 7, 14, or 30 days of behaviour. Send different campaigns to each. The result: smaller sends, higher engagement, more revenue per email.

4. Individual product recommendations

Generic "you might also like" blocks miss. Predictive product recommendations based on each recipient's own purchase history and behaviour hit. Attached revenue per email rises 15 to 40 percent on ecommerce sends with personalised recommendations.

Shopify Magic, Klaviyo predictive recommendations, and Algolia Recommend all do this out of the box. Switch from generic to personalised in one campaign this quarter and measure.

What does not work

  • Heavy personalisation in cold acquisition emails. Subscribers do not know you yet. Looks creepy.
  • Personalisation that ignores send context. Sending a happy-anniversary email to someone who just complained is worse than not personalising.
  • Personalisation tokens that fail and ship as "Hi, %FIRSTNAME%". Test every template before sending.

Honest measurement

To measure the impact of personalisation, run holdouts. Send the personalised version to 90 percent, the generic version to 10 percent. Compare revenue per recipient. If you cannot prove the lift, the personalisation is decoration.

Frequently asked questions

How much does this cost?

If you have a modern ESP, mostly the cost of senior marketer time to design the rules. Tools that do the heavy lifting are already in your stack.

How long to implement?

First win in 30 days (send-time). Full program (all four tactics) in 90 days.

Is hyper-personalisation creepy?

Yes, when it surfaces information the customer did not realise you had. Stay one level above what they would expect. The goal is helpful, not surveillance.

Personalisation moved from a nice-to-have to a baseline. Subscribers compare every email they receive against the best emails they receive. Stay on that bar or fall off the list.

item.title: Content marketing distribution strategies that actually work
item.excerpt:encoded: Great content without distribution is invisible content.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Most content fails because no one sees it. The fix is to spend more on distribution than on creation. Five distribution channels that pay back: email to your own list, paid amplification of your top performers, repurposing into 3 to 5 formats, distribution partnerships, and SEO that targets the right intent.

Content marketers obsess over the content. Distribution gets last priority and the leftover budget. That is backwards. The rule of thumb from senior content teams: spend 30 percent on creation, 70 percent on distribution.

1. Email to your own list

Your owned list is the cheapest, most predictable distribution channel. If you have built one, you have an asset most teams do not. Use it.

Send each new piece of content to the relevant segment of your list within 48 hours of publication. A 5 percent click-through rate on a 10,000-person list is 500 reads, more than most pieces get organically.

2. Paid amplification of top performers

Wait two weeks after publishing. Identify the top 10 percent of pieces by organic engagement. Put paid budget behind those. Do not put paid behind average pieces, they were average for a reason.

Channels: LinkedIn for B2B, Meta for B2C and high-consideration, native ads (Outbrain, Taboola) for top-of-funnel awareness, occasionally Twitter/X for niche audiences. Budget: €500 to €5,000 per piece depending on the asset.

3. Repurpose into 3 to 5 formats

One blog post becomes:

  • A LinkedIn carousel and a thread on X.
  • A short-form video (60 to 90 seconds) for TikTok, LinkedIn, and YouTube Shorts.
  • A podcast segment or a guest podcast pitch.
  • An email newsletter feature.
  • A talking-points doc for sales.

The cost of repurposing is a quarter of the cost of original creation. The reach is multiples.

4. Distribution partnerships

Find five publications, podcasts, or newsletters where your audience already gathers. Pitch them. Offer to write a guest piece, appear as a guest, or sponsor a single issue. The cost is time, the audience is theirs.

Track each partnership. The good ones (top 20 percent) deliver more leads than your own organic. The bad ones teach you to be more selective.

5. SEO targeted at the right intent

Top-of-funnel informational SEO is harder in 2025 because AI Overviews compress click-through. The opportunity is in middle and bottom of funnel: comparison queries, alternative-to queries, and pricing queries. Those still click through, and they convert.

Audit your existing content against the new intent reality. Refresh the pieces that target queries where AI Overviews dominate; either deepen them or repurpose for paid distribution instead of SEO.

What to stop doing

  • Publishing and forgetting. The 24-hour social rotation does nothing.
  • Posting on every platform with the same content. Native formats matter.
  • Treating publication as the finish line. It is the starting line.

Frequently asked questions

How long until distribution shows in pipeline?

30 to 60 days for the first attributable conversions. 12 months for compounding.

How much budget should I allocate to distribution?

Aim for 60 to 80 percent of total content budget. Most teams spend 10 percent. The gap is the opportunity.

Do I need an in-house person for this?

Yes, eventually. For mid-market, one senior content marketer with a third of their time on distribution beats outsourcing the whole thing.

Great content without distribution is invisible content. Reverse your budget split, measure what works, double down on the winning channels.

item.title: Making data-driven creative decisions without killing creativity
item.excerpt:encoded: Data should inform creativity, not constrain it.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Data should inform creative decisions, not constrain them. The teams that get this right use data to set guardrails, identify what to test, and confirm what worked. They do not use data to commission the work. The creative spark stays human.

Two failure modes show up in marketing teams trying to be data-driven about creative. The first: the team builds creative entirely from past performance data, ends up making the same ads everyone else makes, and the metric stops moving. The second: the team ignores data, the work is gorgeous and the campaign tanks. Both happen. Neither is necessary.

How to use data without killing creative

1. Use data to set the brief, not the work

Data tells you what audience to target, what offer to test, what message hierarchy seems to land. It should not tell the creative team "use a green button because green converts." The creative team takes the brief and produces options. Data picks the winner among the options.

2. Identify three things to test, not 50

Multivariate testing on 50 variables produces noise. Pick three meaningful tests per campaign. Run them long enough to reach significance. Move on. The most useful test variables: headline, hero image, primary CTA.

3. Confirm with data, validate with humans

Data confirms the variant that converted. Senior creative reviewers validate that the winner is on brand. If the data winner makes the brand worse, reject it. Brand drift is paid back with lower CAC two years later.

Where data should always inform

  • Channel choice. Where the audience actually is, not where you wish they were.
  • Format choice. Vertical video, carousel, static, audio. Each platform has clear winners.
  • Timing. When the audience is engaged. Predictive send-time, day-part scheduling.
  • Iteration speed. How often to test new creative based on fatigue curves.

Where data is bad at deciding

  • Brand voice. No A/B test makes a voice. That is a senior call.
  • Long-term positioning. Short-term tests reward generic. Long-term positioning rewards specific.
  • Whether to be brave. The best campaigns underperform variants in week one. Data alone kills them too early.

A practical framework

  1. Brief: data sets audience, problem, success metric. Creative leads define the creative response.
  2. Production: 3 to 5 variants on the same core idea, not 50 small variants on a generic core.
  3. Test: live for 7 to 14 days, sample size matters, significance matters.
  4. Confirm: data picks winner. Senior creative review checks brand fit.
  5. Iterate: winner becomes the control, new variants challenge it next cycle.

Frequently asked questions

What if data and creative disagree?

Investigate why. Sometimes the data is noisy. Sometimes the creative is wrong. Sometimes the metric is wrong (we measured clicks, the goal was revenue).

How do you avoid creative drifting into generic?

Hold a quarterly brand review where senior leadership and creative leads compare the last quarter's output against the brand book. Kill anything that drifted.

Should I A/B test brand?

No. A/B testing is for tactical decisions. Brand is a long-term decision. Test campaigns, not positioning.

The teams that perform best treat creative as a craft and data as a tool. The data sharpens the question, the creative supplies the answer.

item.title: Mobile-first marketing strategies for 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: Mobile isn’t the future — it’s the present.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Mobile is not a channel, it is the default. Yet most marketing programs still treat mobile as a port of desktop. The fix is to design every campaign mobile-first: messaging, creative, forms, landing pages, and tracking. The teams that do this see 30 to 60 percent higher mobile conversion.

Mobile traffic crossed 50 percent of total web traffic in 2017. Conversion rates on mobile lagged for years because every marketing asset was made for desktop and resized down. In 2025 the gap is closing, but only for teams that build mobile-first.

What mobile-first actually means

It is not a thinner header, a bigger button, or a hamburger menu. Those are mobile cosmetics. Mobile-first is a design discipline that starts from the smallest viable screen and adds for larger ones, not the reverse.

Five practices that move the conversion number

1. Headline rewrites

Desktop headlines are read. Mobile headlines are glanced. Cut your hero headline to 7 words or fewer. The supporting paragraph should be readable without zooming. Most teams discover their existing copy is 30 to 50 percent too long for mobile.

2. Form shrinking

Every field on a mobile form costs 5 to 12 percent conversion. Forms that worked on desktop (8 to 12 fields) collapse on mobile. Cut to 3 fields for top-of-funnel, 5 for high-intent. Use one-tap inputs (autocomplete, email keyboard, postcode lookups, social sign-in).

3. CTA discipline

One primary CTA above the fold. Always 44 pixels minimum tap target. No competing buttons in the same view. Sticky footer CTA on long pages so the buyer can always act.

4. Page speed under 2.5 seconds

Largest Contentful Paint above 2.5 seconds doubles bounce rate. Compress images, defer non-critical JS, eliminate heavy ad scripts on landing pages. Use the Chrome Lighthouse mobile audit weekly.

5. Click-to-call and click-to-message

For high-consideration services, mobile users want to call or message, not fill a form. Add tel: and sms: links to landing pages and ads. For B2B, click-to-book-a-meeting (Calendly, HubSpot Meetings) often outperforms forms.

Mobile creative differs from desktop creative

  • Vertical format wins on every social platform.
  • Captions on by default for video, since most users watch without sound.
  • Faster hook (under 2 seconds) since the thumb is already scrolling.
  • Bigger text, higher contrast, brand cue in the first second.

How to audit your mobile experience this week

  1. Open the site on your phone. Try to complete a conversion (signup, demo, purchase) in three minutes.
  2. Run Lighthouse on your top five landing pages. Aim for green across Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO.
  3. Watch a session recording from a mobile user via Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity. Note where they thumb-fumble or rage-tap.
